name: Tara Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a family-run agency that covers our village and the ones around it. I borrow Mum's little Corsa most days, and I do five or six calls in the morning and two at teatime. A lot of my clients I already knew from chapel, like Mr Ellis, who's ninety and used to be a deacon. I get him up, help him shave, and he insists on saying grace over his toast even if we're running late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's proper work, looking after people who looked after the village for years. What wears me out is the forms, because I'm slow at writing and I hate the phone the office makes us use. And money's tight. Owen, my fiancé, is a plasterer, and we're getting married next June, so every spare pound is going on the wedding, and some of it's on a credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because I never trusted all that hype. I'd say it after chapel, not online, because I don't really do social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm glad, because I don't want to learn any of it. But it doesn't help with the money. I'm on low pay with a wedding to pay for and a credit card I don't like having.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my rounds the way I always have. I'd cut back, no new clothes, and we'd do the wedding food ourselves with Owen's aunties. I wouldn't touch any AI, because I've never needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but still worried about money. If AI turns out to be hype, I'll still be paying for my wedding on a credit card I'm ashamed of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the credit card. How much is on it, and how do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About nine hundred pounds, which is more than I've ever owed. My parents never had debt, and I feel like I'm letting them down. Owen says it's normal, but it doesn't feel normal to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be looking after older people, if not agencies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families, first. My nan lived with us till she died, and that's how it should be. But people move away for work now, so somebody has to do it, and I'm glad it's people like me and not strangers.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because I never trusted the hype.
I'd say it **after chapel**, not online.
think: I'm **glad**, because I don't want to learn any of it.
It doesn't help with **low pay** and a wedding to pay for.
do: Keep doing my **rounds** the way I always have.
Do the **wedding food** ourselves with Owen's aunties.
Stay away from **AI**, as I never needed it.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, I'll still be paying for my wedding on a credit card I'm ashamed of.
fieldNote: Tara owes about **nine hundred pounds** on a credit card and feels ashamed of it.
She believes **families** should care for their own, as hers did for her nan.
Her chapel ties mean she cares for people she **already knows**.

steps.text: Keep the morning calls starting with Mr Ellis
Cook the wedding food with Owen's aunties to save money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still need people, especially old people. I'd tell the girls at work not to panic, because nobody's going to let a computer wash Mr Ellis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried about keeping up. The office would want everything on the phone, and I'm already the slowest at the forms. I'd worry they'd prefer the younger ones who are quick with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and wait to see what they actually make us do. If I had to learn something, I'd ask my cousin Leanne to sit with me. I'd keep saving for the wedding as best I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, honestly. Like I'm being left behind. Nobody is going to let a computer wash a ninety-year-old deacon, but the office might still prefer the carers who are quick on their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The office already makes you use a phone. What happens if it does more of the thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be checked on more, I think. If I'm late or the notes are short, it'd flag it straight away. Right now Sue in the office is kind about it, because she knows I'm good with the clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Owen say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen would say plastering is safe, because no robot can do a ceiling. He's probably right for now. He'd tell me to stop worrying and keep my head down.

say: I'd say **people still need people**, especially old people.
I'd tell the girls at work **not to panic**.
think: I'd worry about **keeping up**, being slowest at the forms.

do: **Keep going** and wait to see what they make us do.

S1.quote: Nobody is going to let a computer wash a ninety-year-old deacon, but the office might still prefer the carers who are quick on their phones.
fieldNote: Tara's fear is being **left behind** by faster, phone-savvy colleagues.
She relies on **Sue** in the office being kind about her short notes.
Owen's **plastering** feels safe to the couple for now.

steps.text: Carry on with paper-first notes until made to change
Wait to see what the office actually brings in
Ask cousin Leanne to teach any app she must use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and I'd say it plainly. Old people deserve a person, and I'd say so to anyone who'd listen at chapel or the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it means I've got until 2031 and then there's nothing for me. The office side would go first, which might even keep me busy for a bit. But when the robots come, the hands-on work goes, and that's all I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Owen about bringing the wedding forward, small, just family at chapel, and not spend on a big do. I'd pay off the credit card before anything else. I'd lean on family and chapel, because that's what they're for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I don't like to say it, but I would be. I left school at sixteen and found something I'm good at. A machine taking it before I'm thirty-one would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years for thinking AI, five for robots. What does that do to the wedding and your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd make it small and cheap, and maybe do it sooner, so at least we're settled. Children would have to wait, which I'd hate. Mum wants grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you turn for help, if work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then chapel. The minister's wife helps people find work, and Owen's dad has a few contacts. I wouldn't want benefits unless I really had to.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** and old people deserve a person.
I'd say so at **chapel** or the shop to anyone who'd listen.
think: I've got until **2031** and then there's nothing for me.
The **hands-on work** is all I know, and robots would take it.
do: Bring the **wedding forward**, small, just family at chapel.
Pay off the **credit card** before anything else.
Lean on **family and chapel** before benefits.
feel: **Frightened**, though she doesn't like to say it.
S2.quote: I left school at sixteen and found something I'm good at. A machine taking it before I'm thirty-one would break my heart.
fieldNote: Tara would **shrink and speed up** the wedding to feel settled.
She'd delay **children**, though her mum wants grandchildren.
She'd turn to **chapel and family** and avoid benefits if possible.

steps.text: Hold a small chapel wedding sooner instead of next June
Pay off the nine-hundred-pound credit card first
Ask the minister's wife and Owen's dad about other work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really. I'd say old people deserve a person and I'd keep saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a bit better, but I'd still be out of work by thirty-four or thirty-five. I don't see myself learning a whole new job. I'd probably be at home with children by then, hoping Owen's work holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned, pay the card off, and save what we could. I'd keep caring until it stopped. Then I'd look to the family, and maybe help out at chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but not as sick about it. Five years means a few more years of washing and shaving the old men in our village before the robots move in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years instead of two make a difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd try, but I'd be bad at it. I'd rather do something with my hands. I don't trust a computer to tell me how to care for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new technology if you had to, with this much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would have me back at hers if it came to it. And Owen's family have land, a bit, so maybe there's work there. We'd manage.

say: I'd say old people **deserve a person**, not a machine.
I'd **keep saying it** at chapel and in the village.
think: I'd still be **out of work** by thirty-four or thirty-five.
I don't see myself learning a **whole new job**.
do: Have the **wedding** as planned and pay the card off.
Look to **family** and chapel when it does.
feel: Still **worried**, but less sick about it.
S3.quote: Five years means a few more years of washing and shaving the old men in our village before the robots move in.
fieldNote: Tara expects to **lose her job** at the end of five years, no matter what.
She'd rather have **children** and lean on Owen's work than retrain.
Her safety net is **family**, including Owen's family's land.

steps.text: Pay off the credit card before the wedding
Keep caring in the village until the robots arrive
Lean on Mum and Owen's family if work stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no need to panic. People should plan, like my nan did, and not expect the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably have children by then and be part time. I'd be about forty when the robots come. I don't think I'd go back to full-time caring after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married as planned, pay off the card, and save a bit for children. I'd keep caring part time. If there was an apprenticeship in something hands-on, maybe I'd look at it later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but I still don't like it. Ten years gives me time to marry Owen, my fiancé, and have children before a robot does my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you still be caring by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, part time, until the children came. After that I'd see. I'd like to keep doing it as long as there are old people who want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about this picture all right with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots did the heavy lifting, that'd be all right. My back's already sore. But the talking and the shaving and Mr Ellis's grace, I'd want to keep that.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so there's no need to panic.
People should **plan**, like my nan did, and not expect government fixes.
think: I'd probably have **children** by then and be part time.
I'd be about **forty** when the robots come.
do: Get **married** as planned and pay off the card.
Keep **caring part time** and maybe look at an apprenticeship later.
feel: **Calmer**, but she still doesn't like it.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to marry Owen, my fiancé, and have children before a robot does my job.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Tara **build a family** before her work is threatened.
She'd welcome robots only for **heavy lifting**, not the personal care.
Her outlook puts **planning** on families, not government.

steps.text: Marry Owen next June as planned
Save a little each month for starting a family
Keep caring part time in the village

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There'd be no time to get married properly or save anything before the robots came. What would help is more pay now, so I could get out of debt, and a promise that old people can still choose a person. Old people in our village built the chapel with their own hands, and they deserve a real person holding their hand at the end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what families want. Some of the sons and daughters would be glad of a robot, so they don't have to feel guilty. That's what really worries me.

headlineQuote: Old people in our village built the chapel with their own hands, and they deserve a real person holding their hand at the end.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old** carer in her home village, borrowing her mum's car for calls.
She goes to **chapel** and cares for people she has known all her life.
She is marrying **Owen**, a plasterer, next June and has a credit card she's ashamed of.
She never uses AI and moves from anxious to **alarmed** under AGI in two or five years.
Her plan rests on **family**, chapel and starting a family of her own.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to marry properly or save anything.
whatWouldHelp: **More pay now** to get out of debt.
A promise that older people can still **choose a person**.
